walkthroughs.body_html:
Paper 1: Exploring Modern and Literary Heritage Texts — a core area of GCSE English Literature.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Paper 1: Exploring Modern and Literary Heritage Texts brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Paper 1: Exploring Modern and Literary Heritage Texts.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a theme and a symbol?
options: A theme is an abstract idea or concern the text explores (e.g. mortality); a symbol is a concrete image that stands for something else (e.g. a skull).
A theme is the title of the book.
Themes are just symbols repeated through the book.
Gothic refers to medieval architecture, not literature.
When a speaker says one thing but means another — typically the opposite — relying on shared context for the listener to detect the gap.
Gothic refers to medieval architecture, not literature.
Verbal irony is when you make a joke about something.
Verbal irony is just saying something unexpected.

mcqs.q: What are conventions of the Gothic genre?
options: Settings of ruin and decay, supernatural or psychological terror, transgression of boundaries, the sublime, doubled or haunted protagonists, and atmospheric excess.
Gothic just means scary stories with vampires and ghosts.
Gothic refers to medieval architecture, not literature.
A theme is the title of the book.
